steps.caption: Black to move. Look at the white king on h1: two pawns in front of it, and the white queen far away on h5. Black's rook can give check on the first rank. White's last move captured the black queen on b1. Guess before you read on: mate, or only a check?

claims.statement: The rook can go to e1.
Black is not in check and can move.

steps.prompt: Black's rook goes to the first rank with check. Pick a guess and give one reason. The lesson comes back to this position, so write what you actually think.

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Look at any position and decide, with nobody naming the idea, whether a back-rank mate exists, for either side. Refute a mate that is not there. Make your own king safe in the cheapest way. And say plainly when there is no back-rank mate at all. The test near the end mixes positions with and without mates, and nothing in it is labelled.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's rook is on the other side of the board, but the d-file is open. Count the squares the white king could step to.

claims.statement: The king can go to f1 and h1 only.

steps.text: **Shield and cage.** The three pawns shield the king from checks coming from the front, yet they also fill three of its squares. An edge king has at most six squares (its own and five neighbours), and here the pawns take three. Emanuel Lasker's reminder for any attack is to count the squares you must control and to make sure the checking piece cannot be taken.

**How to look for it.** First, find the king and count its free squares: pawns in front of it often fill them. Then look for a piece that can check along the first rank, and ask whether anything can take it. Last, ask whether anything can step between the checker and the king. Three "no" answers mean mate.

steps.caption: The same position, Black to move. Step through and count which squares one rook covers. [H] Counting the squares before hunting for checks may find mates faster; untested.

line.say: One rook check covers e1, f1 and g1. The king cannot step to h1 either: that square lies on the same line.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 covers f1.
The rook on d1 gives check on g1.

steps.caption: An uncastled king is shut in the same way. White to move: which squares are free for the king?

claims.statement: The king can go to d1 and f1 only.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black's rook stands on the e-file, which has no pawns on it.

line.say: The rook checks along the first rank. The pawns hold the king in, and nothing white covers e1.

steps.text: **Three conditions.** A check along the first rank is mate only if all three hold. **One:** the king has no flight square. **Two:** nothing can capture the checking piece. **Three:** nothing can step between the checker and the king. Look at them in that order. Remove any one and it is only a check.

steps.title: What turns a mate into a check?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position: mate, or only a check? Then say what changed.

steps.caption: Back to the opening position. Compare with your guess at the start: what did you miss or get right? Then check the three conditions one by one.

line.say: The rook checks. g2 and h2 fill the king's squares, nothing covers e1, and nothing can step in.

steps.text: **Only a rook?** No. Any piece that gives check along the rank can mate there: a queen as well as a rook, or two pieces working together. The three conditions never change. What changes is how you meet the second one: when a defender can take the checking piece, you may need a second piece behind it. The next three boards show each case.

steps.prompt: In positions B, C and D, which condition failed? Which of the three questions do you usually forget to ask?

steps.caption: White to move. A queen can do the rook's job. Look for the check on the eighth rank.

line.say: The queen checks along the eighth rank. Nothing can take it or step in, and the pawns hold the king.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has two rooks guarding the eighth rank; White has two rooks aimed at it.

line.say: The first rook takes the guard on e8 with check.
The other black rook has to recapture; nothing else can.
The second rook takes again, and now nothing is left to take it.

claims.statement: White mates in two moves, starting with the capture on e8.
The rook on e2 attacks e8.

steps.caption: White to move. A knight guards e8, so a lone rook check would simply be taken. The queen stands behind the rook.

line.say: The rook goes to e8 with check, backed by the queen behind it.
The knight must take it; there is no other reply.
The queen takes the knight with check, and the guard is gone.

claims.statement: The knight on f6 covers e8.

steps.caption: Position A. White to move. Predict before you step: mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks along the eighth rank. Look at each of the three questions.

steps.caption: Position B: one black pawn has moved from h7 to h6. Same question: mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks. The pawn move gave the king a square.
The king steps to h7 and the check is over.

steps.caption: Position C: the black bishop has moved from b7 to d7. Mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks, but the bishop covers e8.
The bishop takes the rook, so the check does not mate.

claims.statement: The rook is lost along the engine line.

steps.caption: Position D: the black bishop stands on d6 and the h-pawn is back on h7. Mate, or only a check?

line.say: The rook checks. This time a piece can step in.
The bishop interposes on f8, and the check is parried.

claims.statement: Two black pieces cover f8: the bishop and the king.

steps.text: **The checklist.** Before you call a check on the first rank mate, ask three questions in order. Where can the king go? Who can take the checker? Who can step in between? If the answers are 'nowhere', 'nobody' and 'nobody', it is mate. If not, say aloud which question failed: flight, capture or block. [H] Naming the failure may help you diagnose your own mistakes faster; this is untested.

**Remember.** A check on the first rank is mate only if the king has no flight square, nothing can capture the checker, and nothing can block. Ask those three questions in order, and say which one failed if it is not mate. A queen can do the job as well as a rook. Many positions have no mate at all. Run the routine: flight, capture, block.
